## Summary Scores

-   **Sensitivity:** Moderate
-   **Exposure:** Moderate
-   **Vulnerability:** Moderate

```{r}
#| echo: false

ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Blueline tilefish")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path,

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {

} else {
```

## Score Descriptions:

### Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Define the directory and the correct file extension pattern
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Blueline tilefish")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path, 
  pattern = paste0("sensitivity.*", ext), 
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Blueline tilefish Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens-blueline
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"

knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

Blueline tilefish received a **Moderate** sensitivity score. Certainty was 90% (@fig-sum-tab-blueline). Three attributes had scores greater than 2.5: Adult Mobility (2.8), Population Growth Rate (2.8), and Historical Variability in Temperature (2.5) (@fig-sum-tab-blueline).

Adult blueline tilefish are primarily demersal. They are thought to be sedentary and remain close to their dens, similar to goldenline tilefish [@schmidtke2017life]. Maximum ages upwards of 50 years have been recorded [@schmidtke2017life] [@spanik2023validating]. They reach maturity anywhere from a few months to 3.7 years off the coast of Virginia to upwards of 5 years off the southeast US [@ross1982feeding] [@harris2004age] [@low2023characterizing].

Blueline tilefish were not included in the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment for the Northeast US, but were included in the recent Climate Vulnerability Assessment for the Southeast US [@burton2023climate]. Blueline tilefish received a High sensitivity score in that assessment. This score was driven by Sensitivity to Temperature and Population Growth Rate attributes. The experts in that assessment suggested that long-lived, slow-growing nature of blueline tilefish are believed to make them susceptible to overfishing [@burton2023climate].

Mean Exposure for Blueline tilefish along the Northeast Shelf was **Moderate** (2.35 +/- 0.85) (@fig-sum-tab-blueline). Exposure was relatively consistent across the species distribution in this region and was driven by high bottom salinity and aragonite solubility exposure (@fig-exp-blueline; @fig-fact-exp-blueline).

Blueline tilefish were not included in the previous assessment on the Northeast Shelf but were recently assessed in the Southeast US [@burton2023climate]. In that assessment they received a Very High exposure score, which was driven by high sea surface temperature, salinity, ocean acidification, and current changes [@burton2023climate].

Mean Vulnerability for Blueline Tilefish throughout its range on the Northeast Shelf was **Moderate** (4.7 +/- 1.70) (@fig-sum-tab-blueline). Vulnerability was consistent throughout its range in the region (@fig-vuln-blueline). 

In the previous climate vulnerability assessment for the Southeast US, blueline tilefish received a Very High Vulnerability score, driven by Very High exposure and High sensitivity scores [@burton2023climate]. Blueline tilefish have not been assessed in the Northeast previously [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Data Quality Metrics

### Life History Data Quality:

Only 63% of data quality scores were greater than or equal to 2, indicating poor data quality. Most attributes had data gaps (mean attribute data quality score \< 2), including Adult Mobility, Complexity in Reproductive Strategy, Egg and Larval Survival and Settlement Requirements, Historical Variability in Temperature, Other Stressors, and Stock Size/Status (@fig-sum-tab-blueline).

### Model Confidence Score:

The mean model confidence score for blueline tilefish was 1.6 (+/- 1.02), indicating that experts had low to moderate confidence in the model. Scores ranged from 0 to 2.5. Experts said that the model captured the distribution of blueline tilefish well, but low sample size and poor sampling of rocky burrow habitats decreased the confidence. The model AUC score was 0.97, indicating excellent predictive performance.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
*Note: For an animated version of this plot, please see the online version of this document.*
:::

Blueline tilefish experienced a significant loss in total habitat area between 1993 and 2023 due to loss of habitat in the Gulf of Maine and on the continental shelf off the coast of Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina. However, core habitat area on the continental shelf break grew significantly over the same time period (@fig-shifts-blueline). The distribution centroid shifted 24 km southwest.

Under near future climate conditions, blueline tilefish habitat is expected to remain similar (@fig-shifts-blueline). The distribution centroid is predicted to shift a further 4 km westward. 

In the recent Climate Vulnerability Assessment for the Southeast Shelf, blueline tilefish received a moderate Distributional Vulnerability Rank due to limited adult mobility, high habitat specialization, and low larval dispersal [@burton2023climate].

### Directional Effect:

The impact of climate change on blueline tilefish is expected to be **neutral**, with 92% certainty in expert scores. It is possible that blueline tilefish biomass may increase with increasing temperatures, as landings in the Mid-Atlantic have been correlated to increasing temperatures [@pinsky2018preparing] [@rogers2019shifting]. However, little research has been conducted on how blueline tilefish will respond to climate change. The Climate Vulnerability Assessment for the Southeast US also predicted that the effect of climate change on blueline tilefish would be neutral [@burton2023climate].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

Little research has been conducted on the response of blueline tilefish to climate change. Rising water temperatures likely drove a rapid increase in landings in the Mid-Atlantic throughout the early 21st century as blueline tilefish distributions expanded north beyond their traditional South Atlantic boundary [@pinsky2018preparing] [@rogers2019shifting]. Blueline tilefish may exhibit a moderately-high risk to achieving optimal biomass and yield due to climate change on productivity [@mafmc2025update]. 

## Life History Synopsis

Blueline tilefish have only recently been found on the Northeast U.S. Continental Shelf. They live in crevices or on ledges on the shelf, shelf break, and shelf slope from Georges Bank to Mexico and the Gulf of America [@schmidtke2017life]. Blueline tilefish are multiple batch spawners and presumably spawn on/near the bottom [@low2023characterizing]. Spawning occurs from March through October in the southern portion range, and May - November in the Mid-Atlantic Bight [@harris2004age] [@schmidtke2017life]. Eggs and larvae are estimated to remain pelagic for 4-6 weeks and depend on currents for transport. Eddies and gyres may provide local retention while the Gulf Stream transports eggs and larvae up the East Coast. It seems likely that substantial numbers of blueline larvae are transported out of the eastern Gulf of Mexico, to the South Atlantic, and from the South Atlantic into the Mid-Atlantic over the course of a few weeks [@sedar2025report]. Juveniles settle to the bottom and occupy benthic habitats around offshore submarine canyons on the shelf edge, constructing burrows in seafloor sediments or within rocks and boulders [@schmidtke2017life]. Juveniles and adults consume a diverse array of benthic invertebrates, including polychaetes, crustaceans, and decapods. Gastropods and copepods have also been observed and are likely consumed when diel vertical migrations bring them close to the seafloor [@bielsa1987food] [@ross1982feeding]. Age at maturity is up to 3.7 years in the Mid-Atlantic and 5 years in the South Atlantic [@harris2004age] [@low2023characterizing]. Maximum age is 37 years, although it is theorized that individuals could possibly reach upwards of 50 years in age [@schmidtke2017life] [@spanik2023validating]. In the Northwest Atlantic, blueline tilefish are managed by the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council under the Tilefish Fishery Management Plan. Council management of blueline tilefish in the Mid-Atlantic began as a response to increased commercial and recreational landings in the region. The Mid-Atlantic stock has not been assessed. Population levels and fishing status are currently unknown but management measures have been in place since 2017 [@mafmc2017amendment].

Bottom temperature, oxygen, salinity, and net primary production were the major dynamic drivers of species distributions along the Northeast Shelf (@fig-radar-blueline). Blueline tilefish are demersal species that occupy the shelfbreak and submarine canyons, so they prefer consistent conditions [@schmidtke2017life]. Blueline tilefish are generalist predators, consuming polychaetes, crustaceans, decapods, and zooplankton [@bielsa1987food] [@ross1982feeding]. When exposure was calculated using only these factors, exposure decreased to Low due to low temperature, oxygen, and net primary productivity exposures (@fig-exp-imp-blueline; @fig-sum-imp-blueline).

```{r}
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| lightbox: true
#| out-width: "100%"
#| label: fig-sum-imp-blueline
#| fig-cap: "As in @fig-sum-tab-blueline for Blueline tilefish, but with only significant Exposure factors and the resulting Vulnerability Scores."
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| fig-align: "center"
knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```
